etymologies.etymologyHTML: From shine +‎ -y (adjectival suffix).

quote.citation: 1920, Will Payne, The Scarred Chin, page 130:
quote.text: He was wearing a new, fawn-coloured summer suit and a new straw hat—his trousers the creasiest and his shoes the shiniest. Yet he seemed not to be taking the usual infantile satisfaction in a very smart, correct costume.

quote.citation: 2011, Ronke Luke-Boone, African Fabrics: Sewing Contemporary Fashion with Ethic Flair:
quote.text: Commercially produced yarn, such as rayon, produces a cloth with a smoother, shinier look than hand-spun cotton, but the uneven, rugged look of hand-spun cotton can be quite appealing.

quote.citation: 2007, Christopher Brookmyre, Attack of the Unsinkable Rubber Ducks, →ISBN, page 132:
1665, John Dryden, Verses to her Royal Highness the Duchess [of York]:
quote.text: Like distant thunder on a shiny day.

When I was bound apprentice in famous LincolnshireFull well I served my master for nigh on seven yearsTill I took up to poaching as you shall quickly hearOh, 'tis my delight on a shiny night in the season of the year.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From shine +‎ -y (noun suffix).

definitions.definition: (slang) Contraction of disparaging term "shiny arses", originating during World War Two, to describe a desk worker.[1]
